newsitem.title: USA: TENNIS-OF SEEDING FRENZIES, OTHER SICKNESS AT 1996 OPEN.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-OF SEEDING FRENZIES, OTHER SICKNESS AT 1996 OPEN.

text.p: It was a repeat for Pete and Graf got it done again, but it was hardly business as usual at this year's U.S. Open.
Before the first ball was struck in anger, Open officials set off a seeding frenzy with the way they conducted the draw.

Men's players were sickened by the way organisers disregarded world rankings and set the rest of the draw before deciding where to seed players. The remedy was pure playground - - a do-over that barely avoided a players' mutiny.
Pete Sampras left his mark on the court. He won his fourth Open despite a staggering quarter-final victory in which he vomited on the green concrete during a fifth-set tiebreaker.
Steffi Graf charged to her fifth Open crown, beating Monica Seles to win the sixth successive Grand Slam tournament she has contested.

Back in Germany, her father, Peter, was spending his 13th month in jail and standing trial on charges of evading some $13 million in taxes on her earnings. A former family accountant, also standing trial, says Steffi was aware of the scheme.
Exit fixture Stefan Edberg. Enter sure-to-be new fixture Martina Hingis, a 15-year-old from Switzerland.

The icy-cool Edberg, 30, celebrated his amazing string of 54 consecutive Grand Slam tournaments with a quartet of victims -- including Wimbledon champion Richard Krajicek -- to reach the quarters in his major farewell before retirement.
The hot-tempered Hingis, petulantly tossing rackets and fuming over line calls, barged into the semifinals before being dismissed by Graf.
Andre Agassi, the main beneficiary of the Open's creative seedings, silenced Thomas Muster, one of the organisers' harshest critics, with a quarter-final spanking.

But then Agassi, ticketed for a marquee championship rematch against Sampras, was beaten as black and blue as his sorry designer tennis outfit by the dashing Michael Chang, who had scampered through a seedless path to the semifinals.
Chang won the French Open as a 17-year-old and reached his first Open final after 10 tries only to find old childhood rival Sampras on the other side of the net.
The two first faced off against one another 17 years earlier on a hardcourt in San Diego, aged seven and eight.
Chang, at last, kept some tradition alive at the Open.
He lost for the ninth time in his last 10 matches against Sampras. And for the fifth time in six Opens, Chang lost to the man who became the champion.
The championships marked the end of an era at the National Tennis Centre complex as we know it.

Louis Armstrong Stadium will be downsized, with the main matches next year to be housed in a new, 23,500-seat stadium next door. The layout of the outer courts is being reconfigured to allow dedicated seating at each court.
No tears were shed at the 1996 championships over the demise of the current concrete complex nestled near the 1964 World's Fair Unisphere in Flushing Meadows park.
One shudders to think, however, how the already lofty price of designer water and barbecued hamburgers at the tournament will be affected by the renovation's $234 million price tag.
